existing_tips: Nationality adjectives agree in gender: français/française, anglais/anglaise. They are not capitaliz
'Venir de + infinitive' means 'to have just done something': je viens de manger = I just ate.
'Beaucoup de' (much/many) is always followed by 'de', never 'des': beaucoup de patience, beaucoup d'
'Avoir chaud' = to be hot (personal feeling). Don't confuse with 'il fait chaud' (the weather is hot
'Il me suffit de' = it suffices for me / is enough for me. Same reverse pattern: il te suffit de, il
Use 'avoir' for physical features: avoir les cheveux bruns (to have brown hair), avoir les yeux vert
'Beau/belle' is one of the BANGS adjectives that go before the noun: 'une belle maison', not *'une m
'À l'aéroport' uses the contracted 'à l'' before vowels. Full form would be 'à le', but that doesn't
Sortir (to go out) is irregular like partir: je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons. Don't confuse
Use 'être' for professions. In French, no article before the profession: Elle est médecin (not 'elle
Aller (to go) is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. 'A
'Sortir' = to go out/leave. Irregular -ir: je sors, il sort. 'Du' = de+le: 'sort du bureau' = leaves
'Avoir' in inversion: 'avez-vous des enfants?' Formal question form. 'Des' = some (partitive).
Watch these: faim, soif, chaud, froid, sommeil, peur, raison, tort, honte, de la chance. All take `a
'Avoir raison' = to be right, 'avoir tort' = to be wrong. French says 'to have reason/wrong'.
'Chez' means 'to/at the place of'. Use with people: chez le médecin, chez moi (at my place), chez Pa
'Où se trouve...?' = Where is...located? More formal than 'Où est...?' Both are correct.
je → j' before a vowel or silent h: j'aime (I love), j'habite (I live). Elision is mandatory – je ai
'Être en retard' vs 'être en avance' (early). Both use 'en' before the noun.
French says 'I have hunger' (`j'ai faim`), not 'I am hungry'. Same with `j'ai soif`, `j'ai froid`, `
'Avoir soif' = to be thirsty. French uses 'to have thirst', not 'to be thirsty'.
Venir (to come) is irregular: je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent. '
'Est-ce que' is the easiest way to form questions – just add it before a statement. No word order ch
Suivre (to follow) is irregular: je suis, tu suis, il suit, nous suivons, vous suivez, ils suivent.
'Aller' is used for health: 'Tu vas bien ?' = Are you doing well? Literally 'You go well?'
'Content' agrees in gender and number: content/contente/contents/contentes. The final -t is silent i
